chunks: Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah narrated from Sharif ibn Sābiq from al-Fadl ibn Abi Qurrāh who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'Indeed, these people say that the earnings of a teacher are *suhṭ* ( consuming wealth/forbidden). He said: 'They are liars, enemies of Allah. They only wanted that the Quran not be taught. And even if a man gave the teacher the blood-money for his son, it would be permissible for the teacher.'

Muad ibn al-Hasan said: 'There is no contradiction between these two reports, because the first report is understood to mean that it is not permissible for him to stipulate a fixed wage for teaching the Quran, and the second report is understood to mean that if something is presented to him as a gift and he is honored with a present, it is permissible for him to take it, and that would be permissible for him.'

key_terms.الْمُعَلِّمِ: The teacher (specifically of the Quran in this context)
key_terms.دِيَةَ وَلَدِهِ: Blood-money for a child, used here as an example of a large sum
key_terms.سُحْتٌ: Consuming wealth or forbidden earnings, often used in contrast to halal income

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible for a Quran teacher to receive payment or gifts according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) refutes the claim that teaching the Quran is *suhṭ* (illicit gain), identifying it as a tactic to discourage religious education. Shaykh al-Tusi clarifies the jurisprudential nuance: while a fixed, stipulated wage (*ajr al-musamma*) may be restricted, receiving voluntary gifts or *iḥsān* is permissible, a distinction supported by later scholars like Ibn Abi Zaynab. This ruling underscores the high value placed on transmitting divine knowledge while allowing for practical sustenance of the teacher.
